primer.e03_p_world.title: A world around a warm sea
primer.e03_p_world.text: You were born into a world wrapped around the Mediterranean. Greek cities, Egypt with its thousand-year-old temples and an ambitious Rome all share its shores. Between 500 BC and AD 200 the stage passes from free city-states and Persian kings to Alexander the Great and his successors, and finally to the Roman Empire. Romans will grow so used to this sea that they simply call it Mare Nostrum, “our sea”. Greek and Latin are the languages of trade and power.
primer.e03_p_world_rome_early.title: The young Republic
primer.e03_p_world_rome_early.text: Around 509 BC, so the story goes, the Romans drove out their last king, Tarquin the Proud, and ever since they have elected two consuls each year. Rome is still a modest town hemmed in by Latins, Etruscans, Volscians and Samnites. Patrician nobles and common plebeians wrangle over power for generations; the plebs win their own champions, the tribunes, and laws written down on the Twelve Tables. Around 390 BC the Gauls sacked the city, yet by the 270s Rome is master of almost all Italy.
primer.e03_p_world_rome_punic.title: Rome against Carthage
primer.e03_p_world_rome_punic.text: Rome has outgrown Italy and reached for the whole sea. From 264 BC it fights Carthage, a rich trading city in Africa. Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants and wiped out a Roman army at Cannae in 216, only to be beaten himself at Zama in 202. In 146 the Romans razed both Carthage and Greek Corinth. Plunder, grain and tens of thousands of captives pour into Rome, and the Senate now decides the fate of kings.
primer.e03_p_world_rome_civil.title: A century of civil war
primer.e03_p_world_rome_civil.text: The Republic is coming apart at the seams. In 133 BC the tribune Tiberius Gracchus, who wanted to give land to the poor, was clubbed to death on the Capitol. Then Marius and Sulla march legions on Rome itself, Spartacus and his army of runaway slaves defeat Roman forces for two years (73–71), and Pompey, Crassus and Caesar carve up power. Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 and was stabbed on the Ides of March in 44. Now Octavian and Mark Antony, with Cleopatra, fight over his legacy.
primer.e03_p_world_rome_augustus.title: The first citizen and his heirs
primer.e03_p_world_rome_augustus.text: After his victory at Actium in 31 BC, Octavian has no rivals left. In 27 BC the Senate named him Augustus; he modestly calls himself princeps, “first citizen”, yet the army, the treasury and the provinces are all his. After a century of war comes the Augustan peace: roads, aqueducts, order. Power stays in the family: Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius, Nero. Under Nero, in AD 64, Rome burned for nearly a week, and in 68 the last of Augustus’s line took his own life.
primer.e03_p_world_rome_empire.title: The Empire at its height
primer.e03_p_world_rome_empire.text: In AD 69 four emperors came and went in a single year, and the winner was Vespasian, a tax collector’s son. His son Titus opened the Flavian Amphitheatre, later called the Colosseum, in 80. Under Trajan the empire reached its greatest size, from Britain to Mesopotamia; Hadrian builds frontier walls and the Pantheon, and Marcus Aurelius writes his philosophical notes in army camps. From 165 the dreadful Antonine Plague swept the empire, and in 193 power fell to Septimius Severus, a man from Africa.
primer.e03_p_world_athens_classical.text: Since the reforms of Cleisthenes in 508/507 BC, Athens has been run by its assembly: thousands of male citizens vote on the Pnyx hill. The city drove back the Persians at Marathon (490) and Salamis (480), led a naval league and grew rich on its dues. Under Pericles the Parthenon rises on the Acropolis, and Sophocles’ tragedies play at the Dionysia. Then come 27 years of the Peloponnesian War with Sparta, defeat in 404 and the execution of Socrates in 399. In 338 Philip of Macedon crushed the Greeks at Chaeronea.
primer.e03_p_world_athens_hellen.title: In the shadow of kings
primer.e03_p_world_athens_hellen.text: After Alexander’s death Athens rebelled and lost: from 322 BC a Macedonian garrison sits in Piraeus, and democracy is cut back and restored by turns. Big politics now belongs to kings, Alexander’s successors, and Athens tacks between them. Yet the city remains the capital of ideas: Epicurus teaches in his Garden, Zeno in the Painted Stoa, which gives the Stoics their name. From 146 BC Rome is the real master of Greece, and young Romans come here to study.
primer.e03_p_world_athens_roman.title: Athens under Rome
primer.e03_p_world_athens_roman.text: In 86 BC Sulla stormed Athens, which had sided with Rome’s enemy King Mithridates, and his soldiers slaughtered many. Since then Athens has been a quiet provincial town with a glorious past, where sons of the Roman elite come to study, as Cicero and Horace once did. Emperor Hadrian adores the city: he finished the colossal Temple of Olympian Zeus, begun more than six centuries earlier, and gave Athens a library. The millionaire Herodes Atticus builds a roofed odeon on the slope of the Acropolis.
primer.e03_p_world_egypt_late.title: The last pharaohs
primer.e03_p_world_egypt_late.text: Egypt is the oldest kingdom on earth: the pyramids of Giza are already over two thousand years old. The last native pharaoh, Nectanebo II from Sebennytos in the Delta, builds temples up and down the land, but around 343 BC the Persian king Artaxerxes III conquers Egypt again. Nectanebo flees south, and the Persians, Greek writers say, loot shrines and carry off sacred books. The Egyptians wait for a deliverer, and in 332 he arrives: Alexander of Macedon.
primer.e03_p_world_egypt_ptolemaic.title: The kingdom of the Ptolemies
primer.e03_p_world_egypt_ptolemaic.text: In 332 BC Egypt opened its gates to Alexander without a fight, and after his death his general Ptolemy seized the country. Macedonian kings rule here now: every man of the dynasty is called Ptolemy, the queens Cleopatra, Berenice or Arsinoe. Temple walls show them as pharaohs, but they speak Greek and live in Alexandria; according to Plutarch, only the last queen, Cleopatra VII, ever learned Egyptian. The farmers of the Nile feed both the royal treasury and Greek cities overseas.
primer.e03_p_world_egypt_roman.title: Rome’s granary
primer.e03_p_world_egypt_roman.text: In 30 BC Cleopatra took her own life, and Egypt became a special province that the emperor governs through a prefect of equestrian rank. Senators may not even set foot here without permission: the land is too valuable. Every summer a fleet carries Egyptian grain to Rome; according to Josephus it feeds the capital for four months a year. Taxes are collected strictly, based on a census every 14 years. In 115–117 a Jewish uprising shook the country, and in 130 Emperor Hadrian came to visit.
primer.e03_p_place.title: Mediterranean shores
primer.e03_p_place.text: Your world is the coastline of a warm sea: rocky hills, olive groves, vineyards and goats on the slopes, and to the south the green Nile valley cutting through the desert. Summers are hot and dry; the rain comes in winter. The real highways are at sea: with a fair wind a ship gets from Rome to Alexandria in two or three weeks, while in winter sailing almost stops. Every town has a temple on a hill, a market square, walls, and tombs lining the roads outside the gates.
primer.e03_p_place_rome_rep.title: City of seven hills
primer.e03_p_place_rome_rep.text: Rome sits on hills by a bend in the Tiber, about twenty-five kilometres from the sea. The Forum, its heart, was once a marsh, drained by a huge sewer, the Cloaca Maxima. Jupiter’s temple crowns the Capitol, a stone wall rings the city, and from 312 BC the paved Appian Way runs south while the first aqueduct brings water in. The more people arrive, the higher the houses climb: the poor cram into rickety multi-storey insulae, the rich live around an atrium, an inner courtyard.
primer.e03_p_place_rome_imp.title: Capital of the world
primer.e03_p_place_rome_imp.text: Rome is the largest city on earth: historians estimate about a million people live here. Augustus boasted that he found it brick and left it marble. Nearly ten aqueducts feed its fountains, baths and rich men’s houses; the Colosseum holds about 50,000 spectators, the Circus Maximus more than 150,000. The streets are crowded, loud and dangerous: apartment blocks five or six storeys high catch fire and collapse, and at night carts rumble through, since they are banned by day.
primer.e03_p_place_athens.title: The city of Athens
primer.e03_p_place_athens.text: The rock of the Acropolis towers over Athens. The Persians burned it in 480 BC, and under Pericles the marble Parthenon rose there with a giant statue of Athena in gold and ivory. Below, the agora hums: market and meeting place, where philosophers argue and fishmongers shout. The Long Walls, some six kilometres, run down to the harbour of Piraeus. All around lies Attica: olive groves, thyme honey from Mount Hymettus and the silver mines of Laurion, whose metal becomes “owls”, coins stamped with Athena’s bird.
primer.e03_p_place_egypt.title: The gift of the Nile
primer.e03_p_place_egypt.text: Egypt is a narrow green ribbon along the Nile between deserts, opening into the broad Delta in the north. Each summer the river floods and leaves black silt behind; Egyptians call their land Kemet, “the Black Land”. Villages are made of mud brick, with dovecotes and shadufs, the long-armed sweeps for lifting water from the canals. And on the coast, from 331 BC, rises Alexandria, a Greek city of straight streets, two harbours and a lighthouse on the island of Pharos, perhaps a hundred metres tall.
primer.e03_p_society.title: Free and unfree
primer.e03_p_society.text: The great divide in this world runs between free and slave; the second, between citizen and outsider. In Athens only male citizens vote, and resident foreigners, metics, pay a special tax. In Rome citizens are ranked into classes by wealth, and the great men keep clients: poorer folk who show up every morning to greet their patron and ask for favours. In Egypt Greeks and Macedonians sit at the top, later Romans, and below them millions of Egyptian farmers.
primer.e03_p_society_slave.title: Born unfree
primer.e03_p_society_slave.text: You were born a slave: in law you are your owner’s property, like a house or a mule. Slaves come from wars and pirate raids and are sold in the markets of Delos and Rome, and a slave woman’s children are slaves too; Romans call them vernae, “home-born”. Mines and big estates are the worst; a town household is easier, where a slave may run the master’s business and save a peculium, money of their own. In Rome a freed slave becomes a citizen, and his son is born free.
primer.e03_p_society_peasant.title: Land and taxes
primer.e03_p_society_peasant.text: You were born into a farming family, like most people in this world. A plot of a few iugera (an iugerum is about a quarter of a hectare) feeds the household: barley or wheat, olives, vines, a couple of goats. In Athens and in republican Rome the farmer is also a soldier who buys his own shield and spear. In Egypt farmers hand a share of the harvest to the king or to Rome, and in flood season they are rounded up to clear canals and mend dykes. A bad harvest, debts or a war, and the plot passes to a rich neighbour.
primer.e03_p_society_noble.title: A noble house
primer.e03_p_society_noble.text: You were born among those who rule. A noble Roman family boasts of consuls among its ancestors: their wax masks, the imagines, are kept in the atrium and paraded at funerals. Under Augustus a senator must be worth at least a million sesterces. In Athens the rich perform liturgies, fitting out a warship or paying for a theatre chorus, and win glory that way. In Egypt the top belongs to Greek courtiers, priests of ancient temples and, later, Roman officials. Nobility here means duty to city and ancestors, and a great deal of money.
primer.e03_p_birth.title: The first days
primer.e03_p_birth.text: A midwife delivers the baby with the women of the family around; men are kept out. By Roman custom, as it is usually told, the father lifts the newborn from the floor to acknowledge it as his own. Girls are named on the eighth day and boys on the ninth; a boy gets a bulla, a charm against the evil eye, a girl a crescent-shaped lunula. Greeks carry the baby around the hearth on the fifth or seventh day and name it on the tenth. Sadly, unwanted infants are sometimes left out in the street, and foundlings are often raised as slaves.
primer.e03_p_childhood.title: Childhood
primer.e03_p_childhood.text: Until about seven you grow up among women, and in a wealthy house with a wet nurse and a slave minder too. Children play knucklebones with sheep’s ankle bones, roll nuts, chase hoops and make dolls of clay and rags. Then boys from families with means go to a reading teacher: in Rome a school is a booth or awning by the forum, in Athens a slave called a paidagogos walks the pupil to class and carries his tablets. Teachers do not spare the cane. Poor children are herding goats or helping in the workshop by seven or eight.
primer.e03_p_home.title: Home
primer.e03_p_home.text: The urban poor live cramped: in Rome, in one room of an insula with no kitchen or toilet, hauling water from a fountain and emptying the chamber pot wherever they can. A rich Roman domus looks inward: an atrium with a pool catching rainwater, a colonnaded garden, painted walls. A Greek house is mud brick on a stone base, with a courtyard and separate women’s rooms. In Egypt people sleep on the flat roof in summer. Light comes from clay oil lamps, warmth from a brazier of coals.
primer.e03_p_food.title: Bread, olives and wine
primer.e03_p_food.text: Grain is the base of every meal: porridge called puls and bread for Romans, barley cakes for Greeks, bread and beer for Egyptians. Add olive oil, beans, lentils, onions, cheese and figs; ordinary people mostly eat meat at festivals, after a sacrifice. Wine is always mixed with water, since drinking it neat is what barbarians do. Romans adore garum, a pungent sauce of fermented fish. The rich dine reclining on couches; the poor buy hot food at street-corner cookshops.
primer.e03_p_clothes.title: Tunic and cloak
primer.e03_p_clothes.text: Nearly everyone wears a tunic, a simple shirt of wool or linen, knee-length for men and ankle-length for women. On formal days a Roman citizen puts on the toga, five or six metres of white wool that you cannot drape without help; senators wear a broad purple stripe on their tunic. Greeks wear the chiton with a himation cloak, Egyptians light white linen. People go in sandals or barefoot. Purple dye is squeezed from sea snails and costs a fortune.
primer.e03_p_faith.title: Gods everywhere
primer.e03_p_faith.text: The gods are everywhere: every house has an altar, every city a patron, every river and grove its own spirit. People offer them grain, wine and incense, and at festivals an ox or a ram, whose meat the whole community then eats. The rule is simple: “I give so that you may give.” For the future you ask oracles and diviners, who read the flight of birds or the liver of a sacrificed animal. Foreign gods are not driven out; they are usually welcomed into the company.
primer.e03_p_faith_rome.title: The gods of Rome
primer.e03_p_faith_rome.text: Every Roman family has a lararium, a household shrine to the Lares and Penates, guardians of home and pantry, who get crumbs from dinner and a few drops of wine. Peace with the gods for the whole city is the priests’ job: the pontifex maximus, the augurs who read the birds, and six Vestal Virgins tending the eternal flame in Vesta’s temple. The greatest temple belongs to Jupiter Best and Greatest on the Capitol. Ritual matters more than feeling: get one word of a prayer wrong and you start again. Before any major undertaking, from elections to war, the gods’ will is read in the birds.
primer.e03_p_faith_athens.title: The Olympian gods
primer.e03_p_faith_athens.text: Athens belongs to Athena: at the Panathenaea, especially grand every fourth year, the city carries a newly woven robe, the peplos, up to her ancient olive-wood statue on the Acropolis. The gods get thigh bones wrapped in fat burned on the altar, while people eat the meat; the myth says Prometheus tricked them into that deal. For advice you travel to the oracle at Delphi, where the Pythia answers in riddles. Once a year at Eleusis initiates enter the Mysteries of Demeter; what is shown there is secret, and revealing it can cost your life.
primer.e03_p_faith_egypt_greek.title: Greek gods on the Nile
primer.e03_p_faith_egypt_greek.text: Your family is one of the Greeks or Romans living in Egypt, and your gods here have grown used to the neighbours. Ptolemy I made Serapis the chief god of Alexandria: bearded like Zeus, yet tied to the Egyptian Osiris and the Apis bull. Greeks pray to Isis as one of their own, and kings and queens are worshipped as gods while still alive. Boys from good families attend the gymnasium, which means sport, Greek festivals and a ticket into the local elite.
primer.e03_p_faith_egypt.title: The gods of Egypt
primer.e03_p_faith_egypt.text: Egypt’s gods are two thousand years older than Rome: Osiris, lord of the dead, his wife Isis, falcon-headed Horus, Amun, Ptah. Kings, native and foreign alike, build them temples at Edfu, Dendera and on the island of Philae, and appear on the walls wearing the pharaoh’s crown. Ordinary people never enter the sanctuary; only shaven-headed priests in linen go inside. But you can buy a mummified sacred animal, an ibis, a cat or a falcon, and offer it to the god; such mummies are buried by the million.
primer.e03_p_faith_judaism.title: People of the Covenant
primer.e03_p_faith_judaism.text: Your family is Jewish. You worship one God who may not be portrayed, rest on the Sabbath, avoid pork, and boys are circumcised on the eighth day. Prayer and the reading of the Law happen in the house of assembly, the synagogue, but the heart of the faith is the Temple in Jerusalem, to which every grown man sends half a shekel a year. Pagan neighbours think Jews odd and stand-offish, but usually let them live by their own laws, and you will keep Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot together with the whole community.
primer.e03_p_faith_judaism_late.title: Without the Temple
primer.e03_p_faith_judaism_late.text: Your family is Jewish, and you live in a world without the Temple: in AD 70 the Romans under Titus took Jerusalem and burned it, and its treasures, even the golden menorah, were paraded through Rome in triumph, as the Arch of Titus shows in stone. The half-shekel Jews had sent to the Temple for centuries now goes to Rome as the “Jewish tax”. The synagogue and the rabbis, sages who interpret the Law, have become the heart of the faith. After the Bar Kokhba revolt (132–135), Hadrian banned Jews from even entering Jerusalem.
primer.e03_p_faith_judaism_alex.title: The Jews of Alexandria
primer.e03_p_faith_judaism_alex.text: Alexandria has the largest Jewish community outside Judea: the philosopher Philo says two of the city’s five quarters are called Jewish. People here speak Greek, and back in the 3rd century BC the Torah was translated into Greek; legend says 72 elders did it in 72 days, giving the Septuagint, “the translation of the Seventy”. The great synagogue was supposedly so packed that a waved cloth signalled when to say “Amen”. Relations with the Greeks are bitter, though: a pogrom broke out in AD 38, and the revolt of 115–117 all but destroyed the community.
primer.e03_p_faith_christian.title: Followers of Christ
primer.e03_p_faith_christian.text: Your family is Christian, following Jesus of Nazareth, who was executed in Judea under Pontius Pilate. There are few of them; on the Lord’s day they meet in private homes, share a meal, sing, baptise newcomers with water and look after widows and the poor as a community. Neighbours whisper about secret night-time gatherings. The law is a threat: in AD 64 Nero blamed the Christians for the fire of Rome and put them to death; under Trajan they are not hunted down, but if someone denounces you and you refuse to sacrifice to the gods, the penalty is death.
primer.e03_p_work.title: Crafts and coins
primer.e03_p_work.text: Almost everyone works the land, yet towns are full of workshops: potters, smiths, fullers and bakers toil in small rooms open to the street, selling right where they work. People pay in coin: the silver drachma in Athens, the bronze as in Rome and, from the 3rd century BC, the silver denarius, the drachmas of the Ptolemies in Egypt. A day labourer earns roughly a drachma or a denarius a day. Ships carry amphorae of wine and oil, Egyptian grain and papyrus. The elite look down on trade and live off land and interest.
primer.e03_p_law.title: Law and courts
primer.e03_p_law.text: Laws here are written down and put on display: the Twelve Tables in the Roman Forum, Solon’s laws on rotating wooden boards in Athens. Courts are crowded: an Athenian jury can have 501 members, each paid three obols a day; in Rome a praetor runs the case and orators like Cicero make the speeches. Punishment depends on who you are: a free man is fined or exiled, a slave is beaten, tortured or crucified. There are hardly any police, so a victim catches the thief himself with the help of neighbours.
primer.e03_p_health.title: Sickness and doctors
primer.e03_p_health.text: Death is a frequent visitor: by modern estimates nearly half of all children never reach adulthood. Fevers abound: malaria in the lowlands around Rome, summer dysentery, plagues that arrive by ship. Greek doctors follow Hippocrates with diets, bloodletting and herbs; surgeons set bones and even remove bladder stones. Many seek healing in a temple of Asclepius, spending the night there and waiting for a dream that will reveal the cure. The rich drink clean water and visit the baths; the poor live in filth and crowding.
primer.e03_p_women.title: A woman’s lot
primer.e03_p_women.text: A girl is married young, at 12 to 15, to an older man, and her father makes the choice. Marriage is about the dowry and children, ideally sons. The wife runs the household, spinning and weaving: wool work is the first female virtue and is even praised on tombstones. Politics and war are closed to women, but priestesses, midwives, market women and estate managers are common enough. Childbirth is the most dangerous thing a woman will ever face.
primer.e03_p_women_athens.title: The women of Athens
primer.e03_p_women_athens.text: In Athens a respectable woman seldom leaves the house: her father answers for her, then her husband, her kyrios, master and guardian. Girls marry at 14 or 15 to men of about thirty, bringing a dowry that goes back to her family if they divorce. On her own she can make a deal worth no more than a medimnos of barley, roughly a sack of grain. Slave women and the poor fetch water and go to market. Yet at festivals like the Thesmophoria and the Panathenaea women stand at the heart of the rites, and the priestess of Athena Polias is among the most honoured people in the city.
primer.e03_p_women_rome.title: The Roman matron
primer.e03_p_women_rome.text: A Roman matron has more freedom than a Greek wife: she dines with her husband, pays visits, goes to the baths and the games, although the law still keeps her under a guardian. She wears the long stola and an elaborate hairstyle. By the late Republic most marriages are made “without the husband’s power”: the wife stays in her father’s family, keeps her own property and can divorce easily. Augustus freed freeborn mothers of three children from guardianship. The most revered women in Rome are the Vestals: thirty years of service, high honour and the best seats at the games.
primer.e03_p_women_egypt.title: The women of Egypt
primer.e03_p_women_egypt.text: Egyptian women have long enjoyed more freedom than their neighbours: they own fields and houses, buy, sell, lend money and inherit alongside their brothers. Marriage is a contract, and papyri spell out what the husband must return to his wife if they divorce. A Greek woman in Egypt formally needs a guardian, a kyrios, yet she too runs her affairs, leases land and goes to court. And women have sat on the throne more than once: Arsinoe II and, in the end, Cleopatra VII.
primer.e03_p_leisure.title: Festivals and shows
primer.e03_p_leisure.text: There are plenty of festivals: the Dionysia with its plays and the Panathenaea with races and contests in Athens; in Rome the December Saturnalia, when slaves dine with their masters, and the games with chariot races in the Circus Maximus. From 264 BC Rome also stages gladiator fights, paid for by rich men buying the people’s affection. Men spend the day at the baths and the gymnasium, playing dice or latrunculi, a battle game on a board. Evenings mean banquets with wine, musicians and dancers.
primer.e03_p_knowledge.title: Letters and learning
primer.e03_p_knowledge.text: Children learn to write on wax tablets, scratching letters with a stylus, while books are copied onto rolls of Egyptian papyrus. Only a minority can read, mostly townspeople and the rich. The Greeks gave the world philosophy: Socrates, Plato and Aristotle debate justice, the soul and the good life. For a career, what matters most is rhetoric, the art of public speaking. Euclid gathered geometry into a single book, Archimedes worked out the law of the lever, and Ptolemy will chart the stars and map the known world.
primer.e03_p_knowledge_alex.title: The Museum and the Library
primer.e03_p_knowledge_alex.text: In Alexandria the Ptolemies founded the Mouseion, the “shrine of the Muses”, where scholars live at royal expense, and the great Library, said to hold hundreds of thousands of scrolls. Legend has it that books were seized from every ship in the harbour, copied, and the copy handed back while the original stayed. Here Eratosthenes measured the Earth’s circumference from a shadow at Syene, and Euclid taught geometry. Egypt keeps its own scripts as well: priests guard the hieroglyphs, and clerks keep records in demotic, a fast cursive.
primer.e03_p_war.title: Wars and armies
primer.e03_p_war.text: War is routine here, almost every summer. Greeks fight in a phalanx: a wall of hoplites with big round shields and spears. Athens is strong at sea, where its triremes, rowed on three levels, ram enemy ships. A Roman legion of about five thousand men is flexible and tough, and each legionary hauls up to 30 kilograms of kit. The Ptolemies even keep war elephants. For the winner war brings loot and slaves; for the losers, burning towns and captivity.
